title: Do children and students have an influence on their own learning?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton surveys six qualities learners bring to their own learning: curiosity, resilience, mindset, social connectedness, a sense of ease, and reflection. For each he gives a short account of why it helps and where it falls short, using personal examples such as shame around maths and a fixed mindset about navigation. He adds a section on intelligence, favouring multiple intelligences and arguing that lower ability slows the pace of learning without stopping it. He ends with two girls inventing a dance at lunchtime who displayed every quality, only to be described by their language teacher as lacking them an hour later. The point is that these dispositions are inconsistent and context-dependent, which prepares his next claim that students should not be blamed for their absence.
points: Curiosity, resilience, mindset, social connectedness, ease and reflection are dispositions that help learners, and none is a given for every child.
Shame erodes a sense of ease and can lead to cheating, lying and quitting even in a student with a growth mindset.
Lower intelligence in an area slows the rate of learning rather than preventing it, and ability-based grouping risks lowering expectations for slower learners.
The same pupils can show every helpful disposition in a self-chosen activity and appear to lack them in class, so these qualities depend on context.
quotes: As children and students go through school, their curiosity levels rise and fall in tune with changes in their brains, their experiences, the subjects on offer to them and their earlier successes and failures. Curiosity does help learning happen, but it is not a given for many of us.

School learning, as opposed to adult learning, is particularly about struggling. Adults often tread water in much of what we do with occasional burst of good or bad struggling as we have to learn something new.

There’s hardly a better description of a student’s school day. It’s why resilience is so important. Resilient children and students, capable of sticking with and pushing through the struggle, have a better chance of learning than those with less resilience.

Mindsets matter because they orient the attitudes children and students bring to their learning. A growth mindset makes the possibility of learning more available and the actuality of learning more likely. A fixed mindset does the opposite.

My lack of ease caused me to lose concentration in math class, to cheat, to copy someone else’s homework on the way home, to lie to my Dad about math and to want to quit. I got through it, but my lack of ease, my shame, slowed my math learning down considerably.

What matters here is to be clear that being less intelligent doesn’t stop learning happening. What more or less intelligence does affect is the time it takes for learning to happen and, therefore, the quantity and quality of learning that is possible within the fixed timescales of schools.

I tell this story just to say that the messiness of learning extends to the qualities and dispositions children and students bring to the process. The very qualities their Spanish teacher wanted them to have I had seen so clearly as they practiced their dance not an hour earlier.
